report.tagline: The only main way to get apps on iPhones and iPads, where Apple reviews every app and takes a cut of digital purchases, now forced by regulators to open up.
report.simpleSummary: The App Store is where iPhone users download apps like WhatsApp, Instagram or games. Apple checks every app before it goes live, and handles payments with your Apple ID. When you pay for something digital inside an app, like game coins or a subscription, Apple has usually kept 15% to 30%. Regulators in Europe, Japan, Brazil and courts in the US have forced Apple to allow other payment options and, in some places, other app stores, which is changing how app makers earn money.

overview.whatItDoes: The App Store is Apple's marketplace for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Watch and Vision Pro apps. Developers pay $99 a year to publish. Apple reviews apps for safety, quality and rule-following, hosts and distributes them, and processes payments. On digital goods, Apple takes a commission. Physical goods and services, like Swiggy food orders or Uber rides, pay no commission.
howItWorks: A developer joins the Apple Developer Program and submits an app for review.
Apple's reviewers check the app against the App Store Review Guidelines, usually within a day or two.
Users find apps through search, charts and editorial stories on the Today tab, plus paid Apple Search Ads.
Digital purchases use Apple's In-App Purchase system; Apple keeps 15% to 30% in most countries.
In the EU, Japan and Brazil, developers can use alternative payments, link out to the web, or use other app stores under new fee terms.
In the US, courts have forced Apple to let apps link to cheaper web payments; what Apple can charge on these is still being fought in court.
overview.valueProposition: For users: safe, easy apps with one-tap payments and easy refunds and subscription control. For developers: access to over a billion high-spending iPhone users, with payments and distribution handled.

businessModel.summary: Apple makes money from the App Store by taking a commission on digital purchases and subscriptions, charging developers a yearly fee, and selling search ads. It is one of the most profitable businesses in the world because Apple controls the only main way to install apps on iPhone, and costs are low compared with revenue.

revenueStreams.detail: 15% to 30% globally; new lower and different rates in the EU, Japan and Brazil.
Developers pay to rank higher in App Store search.
5% on digital sales, even through rival stores, from October 2026.

businessModel.pricing: Standard: 30% on digital purchases, 15% for developers earning under $1 million a year and for subscriptions after the first year. EU from 1 October 2026: 26% In-App Purchase, 20% alternative payments, 15% web link-out, 5% for rival store distribution; 10% to 15% in special programmes. Developer fee $99 a year.
costDrivers: Legal and regulatory costs and fines
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a ₹499 a month subscription bought through In-App Purchase in India. In year one, Apple keeps 30%, about ₹150 a month; from year two, 15%, about ₹75. Payment and hosting costs Apple only a few rupees, so most of that is profit. For the developer, the same user paying on the web would cost only about 2% to 3% in payment fees. That gap, about ₹130 a month, is why developers fight Apple and why regulators step in.

howTheyGetUsers: Every iPhone and iPad comes with the App Store

whatBringsUsersBack: Purchases tied to the Apple ID, so switching to Android loses them
growth.moat: The App Store's moat is control: on iPhone, Apple decides how apps get installed and paid for. Over a billion active iPhone users who spend more than Android users make the store essential for any developer. Regulation is the main force weakening this moat.

pmLessons: Platform rules are product decisions; fees and review rules shape what apps get built.
Controlling distribution is powerful, but too much control invites regulators.
Trust is a feature: safe payments and easy cancellations raise users' willingness to buy.
When regulation changes, the business must redesign pricing without breaking user trust.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Apple lower its App Store commission globally?
interviewQuestions.hint: Revenue impact vs regulatory risk, developer goodwill, user prices. Model scenarios and propose a middle path.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you improve App Store search?
interviewQuestions.hint: User goals, problems (ads, copycats), ideas (better ranking, verified badges). Metric: search-to-kept-app rate.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure the impact of EU changes on developers?
interviewQuestions.hint: Share of payments outside Apple, developer earnings, user prices, adoption of rival stores.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the north star metric for the App Store?
interviewQuestions.hint: Users keeping apps they download or pay for. Break into users, quality downloads, paying users, developer success.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a better onboarding for new developers in India.
interviewQuestions.hint: Persona, barriers (fees in dollars, review), ideas (local pricing help, guides). Metric: first app approved within 30 days.
